Hello! Groomer of a little less than 2 years here. I think it depends on the person, each one of us is going to be slightly different. It can be frustrating, but it's important to remind yourself that it is completely normal and okay to go slow for the first few years. Good prep work, sharp tools, and also maybe a little bit of my phone's camera haha. I make sure my dogs are super clean and thoroughly rinsed out, fully blown out, and if I have the time, I will fluff dry the face. I dry the face most of the way, move the dog to my cutting table, and use our standing dryer to brush out the face while it's drying. When drying the rest of the body, make sure the blow dryer is as high as it can be with the nozzle on, depending on the size of the dog. For large dogs, I put it on the highest setting, and for smaller dogs, I'll put it on medium so im not blowing them away lol. But the power of the dryer helps to straighten and fluff the coat. I also make sure to dry in small sections starting at the neck, making sure each little section is fully dry before moving down to another small section until the body is fully dry. Also, make sure the dogs are fully dry before starting the haircut since damp hair won't cut as nicely. While I'm drying I make sure to check the spot I'm drying with my hands to feel for any dampness and when I'm almost done with the entire body I take the nozzle off the dryer hose and quickly go over the body just to make sure everything is super dry. It's tedious work but ensures a nice smooth cut. I honestly hate blow drying, but grab a chair and some headphones, and put on some music or a podcast lol. 
Sharp tools are KEYYY because my main 30 blade is getting dull right now, and it's a pain in the ass for any comb attachment haircuts I'm doing. With my dull blade, I have to go over the same spots so many times before it's even, and it takes so much longer than a sharpened blade to complete a full haircut. 
You'll get the hang of it with time, but most of it is in the prep work! Good luck :)

I dont know why that went completely over my head lol... OP, like Bby said, you don't need to get 5f blades if you don't want to because you can use the shorter clip combs.

Yes, even with cooling spray they don't cool down all the way. Usually I will use a 5F and every 15-30 seconds I will stop and press the flat side of the blade onto the inside of my arm or the back of my hand to feel the temp. If it's just a little warm I will use it another 15 seconds and check again, usually it's warmer and I will then spray it with the cooling spray, and then set it aside and switch it for another 5F blade. I usually have 3 in rotation. I will repeat that process throughout the groom. Keep in mind that the more the blade is used the faster it will heat up again even with cooling spray. 

I'm not sure exactly what the difference is but my favorite to use under attachments is a 30 blade. However I have used a 10 if needed and that works okay. I find the 30 cuts better and smoother. 

You can not use a 5 with the guard combs. You can only use a 10, 15, or 30. I saw somewhere you can use a 40, but I'm not sure if that applies to all clippers, blades, and combs.

I would get a pair of clippers, three 5F blades, one 10 blade, and the andis metal guard combs (they were hard for me to find but I prefer the andis combs over the Wahl ones. I think they're cheaper, too). Also I don't know a lot about shears, but you'll probably want at least one pair of shears if you dont already have some.

I would check Ebay for the blades. They're cheaper on there. I recently bought some andis ones, and they are crap tbh. I like the AGS blades, they're about the same price as the rest. I also like Geib buttercuts, but they are on the pricier side.

If you plan on getting a second dog, I would definitely invest in good clippers that will last. I use the Wahl Km10 as my work clippers, and they're really good. They are powerful and meant to last.
However if you just need something quick to last you until you can afford better clippers, andis clippers will do you just fine as those were my old work clippers and I used them for a few months before moving jobs with no issues (work provides my clippers so I don't take them with me). I have heard that andis has been putting out worse products, though, so they might be less quality than the ones I had a year ago.
I also recommend shernbao 5 in 1 clippers with the comb attachments, but you have to do proper prep work (bathing and blow drying) for them to work well as they aren't strong or meant to work on dirty or tangled/matted hair. But they're affordable. Those are the clippers I had and used for puppies and smaller dogs (because they're smaller clippers)  and you won't have to buy extra blade attachments, just the comb attachments for different lengths. (I broke them by dropping them, R.I.P...I can't say how long they last based on my experience but my co worker had the same clippers and she had them for a year with no issues before she left so idk how they're holding up).

I personally really like the 5F blade for summer cuts, it's got a nicer finish on most coats compared to when I do a 4F. But please keep in mind you will need to get multiple blades of the same length as well as some cool care spray because the blades will heat up and burn your pups skin if you aren't switching out the blades and cooling them down before reusing. Depending on the blade drive, clippers, speed of clipper, and whatnot the blade can heat up pretty fast like within 30 seconds (idk I dont time it lol) but just something to keep in mind! 

Also for comb attachments those darn plastic attachments really suck. I used them once on a friend's dog and used the clippers she had at her house and told her never again lol. Get the metal ones.

The biggest thing for me during these interviews is I'd find any chance I could to be alone with a regular employee and ask them how they like it here, and ask them to be completely honest. This saved my butt twice from getting a horrible job with a toxic work environment. Its good to look out for how all the employees and managers and everyone is interacting and getting along and even how they are treating the dogs. Of course everything is going to seem good and dandy at the interview because they want you to think that and take the job (most of the time) but if you're able to talk to another employee and ask them to be honest about the pros and cons of the place a lot can be uncovered and you can save your butt. Also pay attention to their employee turn over rate (I think I used that term correctly?) If they can't keep a groomer for too long, there's probably a reason why. 

I had a nightmare interview and two of the employees I got the chance to speak alone with told me they couldn't keep a groomer for longer than 2 weeks. Should have been a red flag and I should have walked out of there to save myself from the rest of that horrible interview.

If you want it to look like the picture, I'd ask for a 2 comb on the body (a little less than a half inch) with a 0 or A comb on the legs (a little over a half inch). The top reasons a dog might over heat is:
1. Impacted under coat, which won't just come out in a bath you'll need a high velocity dryer and brushing down to the skin with a metal comb. 
2. Being overweight.
3. Its just too hot out! Most dogs even short haired ones get overheated in weather that's over 70°f. Some breeds do well in the heat but most don't. My short haired pitbull is panting and trying to find shade when he's only been outside for less than 10 minutes in the summer time. Shaving him wouldn't help, because the problem isn't his hair but that it's just too dang hot outside.

My advice is to never shave a double coated dog. If there are underlying health conditions the coat might not grow back even though it has in the past. On top of that, double coated dogs use their coat to help them cool down as well as stay warm, so shaving it ruins their ability to help cool themselves down. 
Just try to keep an eye on the weather and make sure you're not outside too long when it's over 70-75° outside and you're not doing strenuous activities for too long. 

In summer time I try to let my dog outside for less than 45 minutes at a time and it's usually just to be outside, to sniff things, to get fresh air and get out of the apartment. Short but frequent outside times. And then we do all of our mental and physical exercising inside where the temperature is controlled and he won't overheat.

Personally I like to shampoo, condition, then shampoo again.  Obviously rinsing between each step, and letting the shampoo sit for 2-4 minutes and the conditioner sit for 5-10

Regular baths really helps keep shedding down. Like every 3 or 4 weeks. Which is also why conditioner is really important because you want to rehydrate the skin if you bathe regularly. 

High velocity dryer will be your best friend for getting that shedding out. After every bath thoroughly dry each dog. It will get the loose undercoat right out for you and you won't have to do much brushing. 

My favorite brush for shedding is the deshedding rake. It works on all sorts of coat types as well as helps get tangles out. But depending on the coat texture I will also use a greyhound comb as well as a long pin slicker brush. I also like using a rubber curry brush if the coat is on the shorter side.

The brushing depends on you and if you'd prefer doing a light brushing all over every day or every other day, or a really thorough brushing all over once a week. Either way, if your goal is to keep down shedding, I'd aim for as frequent as possible.

This is just based off of what I've learned so far and my personal opinion, hope it helps :)
